newsitem.title: UK: British leaders slam Germany's Kinkel over Europe.
newsitem.headline: British leaders slam Germany's Kinkel over Europe.

text.p: British political leaders told German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Monday that it was up to British voters to choose their own government after he had urged Britain to commit itself to a future in the European Union.
Kinkel's New Year message, in which he warned Britain that it must make a choice on whether it wants closer integration with the EU, reopened old divisions here over Europe.
Britain must hold a general election by next May and Europe is a key issue for Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party.
"The country must reach a clear decision on its European policy. Britain belongs to Europe. Europe needs Britain," the German minister said.
Alistair Darling, Labour's finance spokesman, said: "It is up to the British people to choose their next government.

"Klaus Kinkel's comments are a kind of desperate message from Europe that there is a British case to be put and that British case is not being put just now because the Conservatives have weak leadership."
Darling's comments were echoed by Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats.
"I think Klaus Kinkel's comments are unhelpful and almost certainly unwise. The British people are perfectly capable of making up their own minds," Ashdown said.
Former Conservative prime minister Sir Edward Heath, who took Britain into Europe in 1972, said Kinkel's remarks reflected intense frustration over Britain's hesitancy over Europe.
Heath said on BBC radio that it was clear that the German government wanted "a British government which is positive".
Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney sought to turn Kinkel's comments to his own electoral advantage.
Britons would have to decide whether they wanted to elect Major, who would "defend British interests" in Europe, or Labour Leader Tony Blair, who would "do what the other European leaders tell him".
Kinkel's comments came at the top of a list of important events likely to shape German foreign policy in 1997.

He renewed earlier affirmations that the planned single currency -- one of the most controversial aspects of EU membership for Britain -- would happen and that preparations would continue through 1997.

He also called for renewed efforts to ensure the success of efforts to streamline EU decision-making and reduce individual countries' veto powers -- another source of irritation to British "Euro-sceptics".
